{{Short description|American experimental physicist (1927–2013)}}
'''Kenneth Radford Shoulders''' (March 7, 1927 – June 7, 2013) was an experimental physicist. He is known for various work related to the field of energy and has also been credited as an early pioneer of electron beam lithography, which has become a key mask-making technology for modern [[microelectronics]].<ref name="OMNI Magazine">{{cite journal|last=Davies|first=Owen|title=Volatile Vacuums|journal=Omni|date=February 1991|volume=13|issue=5|page=72|issn= 0149-8711|url=https://archive.org/stream/omni-magazine-1991-02/OMNI_1991_02#page/n25/mode/2up/search/shoulders|access-date=21 July 2013}}</ref><ref name="Vacuum Microelectronics">{{cite book|last=Zhu|first=Wei|title=Vacuum Microelectronics|year=2001|publisher=Wiley-Interscience|isbn=978-0471322443|pages=2, 181|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yx6Ads0Cb4wC&q=SHOULDERS+VACuum+microelectronic&pg=PA2}}</ref>  He has additionally been attributed the title, ‘Father of Vacuum of Microelectronics’<ref name="Vacuum Microelectronics" /><ref name="The Economist" />  and been known as a founder of microelectronic field emission devices.<ref name="Ball Lightning Study">{{cite journal|last=Davis|first=Eric W.|title=Ball Lightning Study|journal=Air Force Research Laboratory|date=May 2003|pages=26–37|url=http://www.foia.af.mil/shared/media/document/AFD-091008-049.pdf|access-date=21 July 2013|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111117101602/http://www.foia.af.mil/shared/media/document/AFD-091008-049.pdf|archive-date=17 November 2011}}</ref>

==Career==
In the 1950s, Shoulders worked as a researcher at MIT in applied research on microminiature data-processing components and systems, and worked with [[Dudley Allen Buck]] in making thin-film cryotron integrated circuits.<ref>[[Dudley Allen Buck]]</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=RESEARCH IN SELF-ORGANIZING MACHINES|url=http://www.sri.com/sites/default/files/uploads/publications/pdf/1310.pdf|work=SRI Proposal for Research|access-date=21 July 2013|archive-date=28 September 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130928104752/http://www.sri.com/sites/default/files/uploads/publications/pdf/1310.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/201202/physicshistory.cfm |title=This Month in Physics History |publisher=Aps.org |access-date=2013-12-11}}</ref>  In 1958, he moved to California to work as a Senior Research Engineer, [[Applied Physics Laboratory]] created by [[Charles Rosen (scientist)|Charles Rosen]] at [[SRI International|Stanford Research Institute (SRI)]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=D. A. Buck, K. R. Shoulders|title=An approach to microminiature system|journal=Proceedings of the Eastern Joint Computer Conference, Amer. Inst. Of Elect. Engrs|year=1958|pages=55–59|url=http://dl.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=1458057}}</ref> Shoulders established SRI’s microelectronics program.<ref name="Jaehnig">{{cite journal|last1= Jaehnig|first1= Kenton G.|first2=Jacob |last2=Roberts|title=The Frontiersman|journal=Distillations|date=2015|volume=2|issue=3|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/distillations/magazine/the-frontiersman|access-date=16 March 2017}}</ref>   Early in his career at SRI, Shoulders made the first 12 [[Quadrupole mass analyzer|quadrupole mass spectrometers]]<ref name="Hubschmann">{{cite book|last=Hubschmann|first=Hans-Joachim|title=Handbook of GC/MS: Fundamentals and Applications|year=2008|publisher=Wiley-VCH|isbn=978-3-527-31427-0|page=5}}</ref> and then later worked with others such as mouse inventor, [[Douglas Engelbart]] and [[Jerre Noe]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Markoff|first=John|title=What the Dormouse Said: How the Sixties Counterculture Shaped the Personal Computer Industry|year=2005|publisher=Penguin|location=US|isbn=978-0-670-03382-9|pages=[https://archive.org/details/whatdormousesaid00mark/page/16 16–17]|title-link=What the Dormouse Said}}</ref>

During his time at SRI, Shoulders also worked on ideas for a flying  car, the Gyrodyne Convertiplane. It combined the features of a car, a helicopter (a rotor on the roof for take-off and landing) and a small airplane (rigid wings and a rear propeller). Shoulders developed preliminary sketches and specifications, promoting the idea of a ground-to-air vehicle that could rescue long-distance commuters from hours of grid-lock traffic. In 1963, Shoulders asked the [[California State Senate]]’s Transportation Committee for permission to use his invention on public roads, and in 1964 they agreed. However, a number of nearby municipalities banned the Convertiplane from their airspace.<ref name="Jaehnig"/>

Unable to commercialize the flying car, Shoulders created his own company, Vertitek, and began developing remote-controlled drones. He imagined a wide variety of drone applications, from children's toys to agricultural crop dusters. One example, the Boomerang, sent out sound waves to detect and avoid collisions, and looked like giant maple seed.<ref name="Jaehnig"/>

In the 1980s, Shoulders moved to Austin, Texas to work at Jupiter Technologies as Chief Inventor and focusing on electron condensed charge technology (referred to as EV's) along with [[Harold E. Puthoff]].<ref name="Jaehnig"/><ref name="The Economist">{{cite news|title=Does Jupiter have new bolts?|newspaper=The Economist|date=October 1989|volume=313|issue=7624|page=99}}</ref>

In 2000, Shoulders' work related to high energy electron charge clusters was incorporated into a Future Energy Technologies briefing presented to The U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.
